quote: Believe it on the first day, not the third.
what_it_buys_you: Two days. That is all, and it is everything. Those are the only two days when the roads are open, the shops have stock, the taps run and nobody has started deciding who to keep out. Every advantage in this book is downstream of acting while things still look normal. The people who came through the first month had all done the same unremarkable thing: they took an unconfirmed report seriously enough to change their afternoon.
what_ignoring_it_costs: By the third day the decision is made for you and every option left is worse. The petrol stations are dry. The road out is a car park with people walking between the lanes. What you would have bought for money on Tuesday you now have to ask a stranger for, and he has learned things about strangers since Tuesday. There is no version of the third day that is better than the first. Not one.

quote: Fill everything that holds water before the pressure goes.
what_it_buys_you: Nine days for a household, if you fill the baths as well as the pans. Mains pressure outlasts the news by roughly a day and a half, because the towers stay charged for a while after the pumps stop, and that day and a half is a gift nobody thinks to open. Water is the shortest clock you own. Everything else on your list can wait behind it.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will be walking to open water inside a week, in company, carrying containers, and every one of those words is a danger on its own. The walk is where people meet each other badly. Sam calculated it once on the back of a feed bill. An hour of filling on the first morning saves you about forty miles of walking in the first month, and the forty miles are the part that kills you.

quote: Do not go to the hospital.
what_it_buys_you: Your life, in the first week, and I have never heard this rule seriously argued against by anybody who was in one. A hospital in the first days is the whole population of a district funnelled through four doors, sorted by nobody, at close quarters, in a building nobody can lock. It is the worst room in the county and every instinct you have is pulling you towards it.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Marta went in on the second morning because she was a nurse and it did not occur to her to be anywhere else. She came out on the fourth. Of the people she went in with, she could name two who came out at all. Whatever you have that needs a hospital, the honest arithmetic is that the building will not treat it and will give you something worse. Find a nurse. Do not find a ward.

quote: Take the shoes, not the photographs.
what_it_buys_you: Working feet in the second month, which is not a small thing when everything you do from then on is walking. Boots that fit, two pairs of thick socks, and something waterproof beat every sentimental object you own put together. The rule is about how to pack when you have nine minutes and a panic on you: hands first, feet first, then heat, then food, then water, then paper.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Blisters, then a wound, then a fever, then chapter five. I have watched a man walk out of a burning village carrying a wedding album and no coat. By the end of the week the album was in a hedge. It was heavy and he had nothing to keep the rain off. Take the photographs on the second trip. There is often a second trip. There is never a second pair of feet.

quote: Write down where you have gone and leave it where they will look.
what_it_buys_you: The chance that your family finds you, which in the first fortnight is better than most people think, because everybody is moving to the same handful of predictable places. A note on the kitchen table, the date on it, the road you took and the name of where you are heading. Joyce added one line to the school list that put families back together for two years: name the second place too, in case the first one is gone.
what_ignoring_it_costs: People who did not leave notes spent the first winter walking. Not searching, walking, in circles, between the four places they thought the others might be, using up the only good months on a problem that a pencil solves. Two of them died on those roads. The note costs you a minute and it is the cheapest thing in this book by a distance.

quote: Get off the main roads before dark on the first night.
what_it_buys_you: A night without other people. The A roads on the first evening are a slow river of cars with families in them. All of them are frightened. None of them have eaten. Every one of them is watching what is in the back of your vehicle. Nothing on that road is moving faster than a walk by nine o'clock. The lanes are empty and they go to the same places.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will spend the night stationary in a queue, in the dark, with your engine off to save fuel and your doors locked, which is where the first robberies happened and where the first fires started. The block at Long Preston held for eleven hours and then collapsed, and the people who died there died in cars, in a line, three miles from a lane they knew.

quote: The radio is worth more than the car by the third day.
what_it_buys_you: Information you cannot get any other way, for about a fortnight, and after that the far more useful knowledge of who else is still broadcasting and from where. A wind-up set and a car battery with an inverter will outlive every phone in the house. In the first week the six o'clock bulletin was the only thing telling people which valleys were closed, and it was right more than it was wrong.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You make your decisions from rumour brought by people who have an interest in what you do next. That is how three families ended up walking towards Preston in the second week. Somebody told them there was a centre there. There was no centre. There had been an announcement about a centre, four days earlier, and the announcement had been cancelled the same evening on the radio nobody had.

quote: Lock the door behind you even when you are coming straight back.
what_it_buys_you: It costs four seconds and it removes an entire category of disaster, which is coming home to a house that has something in it. In the first week this feels absurd. You are carrying a box to the car. You will be ninety seconds. Tom locked the parlour door every single time for three years, including the times he was standing outside it, and he never once had to clear his own building.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Clearing a house you already live in, with your family standing in the yard, in the dark, and no way of knowing whether the thing you can hear is upstairs or in the cellar. The four seconds are not about the door. They are about keeping the habit alive on the days when nothing is wrong, so that it is still there on the day something is.

quote: You are allowed to decide it is nothing and go home.
what_it_buys_you: Permission to be wrong, which you will need, because most alarms are nothing and a person who cannot stand down will burn out inside a month. Nell was fifteen and said this to a yard full of adults who had been awake for two days on a rumour. Go to bed. It is a dog. It was a dog. The rules in this chapter are cheap insurance, not a way to live, and a household that treats every noise as the outbreak will be exhausted before the outbreak arrives.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Nothing, on the day you stand down wrongly and lose an afternoon. Everything, on the day you are too tired to think because you have not slept properly in three weeks. The whole of chapter one is about spending caution while it is free. This last rule is the reminder that by the second month it is not free any more, and you will have to start choosing.

quote: Decide your trigger before you need it, and write it down.
what_it_buys_you: A decision made by the version of you that has slept. The trigger has to be a fact you can check and not a feeling: the mains go off, the second house on the row empties, you hear one in daylight. When the fact arrives you do not deliberate, you execute, and the whole terrible internal argument has already been settled weeks ago by somebody calmer wearing your clothes.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will make the biggest decision of your life while your hands are shaking, in a house full of things you love, with somebody asking you a question. Nobody does that well. The consistent pattern in the first month is not people leaving too early. It is people leaving four days late, on foot, having missed the window when the vehicle would still have got them there.

quote: Leave in daylight or not at all.
what_it_buys_you: Sight, which is the entire game. In daylight you can see a blocked road from four hundred yards, read a junction, spot the group at the bridge before it spots you, and turn around with room to do it. Deniz drove lorries for nineteen years and his whole philosophy came down to one line: the dark does not hide you from them, it only hides them from you.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Night driving after the first week means arriving at every problem at the moment you are closest to it. The road out of Bracewell was cut by a fallen tree at head height across a bend. In daylight it is a nuisance and you reverse. Four families hit it in the dark over two nights. If your trigger fires at nine at night, you lock the door and you go at first light. Waiting eight hours is not the same as waiting four days.

quote: Everything you carry has to go six miles uphill.
what_it_buys_you: An honest packing list. Load the bag, put it on, walk to the end of the lane and back with it, and it will tell you the truth in about ten minutes. What survives that test is water, food, a blade, cordage, a means of fire, a means of boiling, dry socks, a coat and a bag of medicine. Aiden had a rule for anybody hesitating over an object: if you would not carry it up the fell for somebody else, leave it.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will decide what to abandon while exhausted, on a road, in front of people who are watching you do it. That is how good equipment ends up in hedges and how people arrive somewhere with a full pack of the wrong things. The other cost is speed. A man carrying forty kilos walks at two miles an hour and cannot run at all, and there are afternoons when the ability to move quickly for ninety seconds is worth more than everything in the bag.

quote: Take the map, not the phone.
what_it_buys_you: Every lane, ford, footpath, farm track and contour line in the district, in your hands, in the rain, for years, without power. A paper sheet lets you plan around the roads everybody else is on. The ability to move by tracks that do not appear on a road atlas is the largest tactical advantage available to a person on foot in this country.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Roads. You will move on roads because roads are what you can remember, and roads are where everybody else is. By the second week roads have people on them who are waiting for people like you. Joyce took eleven Ordnance Survey sheets out of the school cupboard on the first Friday and they have routed more journeys than anything else we own. Nobody has ever asked me for a phone.

quote: Siphon on the way out, not on the way back.
what_it_buys_you: Range while range still matters. In the first fortnight there is fuel in every driveway in the county and it is nobody's, and the tanks are full because people topped up in the panic and then never went anywhere. Take it as you pass. A jerry can filled on Tuesday is forty miles you can spend later on a decision you have not had to make yet.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Petrol goes off. It is stale in six months and useless in a year, and the water in the bottom of an abandoned tank arrives at the same time. The people who thought of fuel as a thing they could come back for came back to varnish. There is a window of about three months when the whole county is a fuel depot, and it closes without any announcement.

quote: A vehicle is a loud room with windows.
what_it_buys_you: The right relationship with the thing that feels safest. A van gets you eighty miles. Then it is a metal box that announces you for half a mile in every direction, cannot leave the road, and cannot be defended by the people inside it. Use it hard and early for distance, and stop thinking of it as shelter the moment you arrive.
what_ignoring_it_costs: People sleep in cars because a car has doors and doors feel like a house. Elin found a family who had done it in a lay-by above Wigglesworth, and they had done everything else right. The windows are the problem. You cannot see out at night and everything can see in, and a car park is a place other people also think of as safe. Sleep in a building with two exits, or in a hedge, and leave the vehicle where it can be reached without walking into the open.

quote: Have a second destination, and tell nobody outside the house what it is.
what_it_buys_you: Somewhere to go when the first place is burnt, occupied, or full. Half of all journeys in the first month failed on arrival, and the families who had a second name in their heads turned around inside an hour. The ones who did not stood in a yard arguing until dark, which is how people end up sleeping somewhere they have not chosen.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Improvisation at the worst moment. The second half of the rule is harder and it is the half people break. A destination that four groups know about is a destination four groups will walk to when their own plan fails, and none of them will be arriving in a good mood. Tell your household. Tell whoever you would want to find you. Beyond that, say you are heading north.

quote: Go back for the animals once.
what_it_buys_you: A decision you can live with, and a limit on it. Elin was a large animal vet and she understood better than anybody what it costs a person to walk away from stock in a shed. So the rule is not do not go back. It is go back once, in daylight, with somebody watching the road, and open every gate you can reach before you leave. Opened gates are the difference between a slow death and a chance.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The second trip is where people die, and the third is where they die having achieved nothing. The pull increases rather than fades. Elin went back four times to a practice in Settle for drugs that were already gone by the second visit. She said afterwards that she had not been going for the drugs since the first time. Know what the journey is actually for. Then go once.

quote: Staying is a decision too, and for some people it is the right one.
what_it_buys_you: Ground you know in the dark. Tom never left Hillfoot and is the reason a good deal of this book exists. A farm with its own water, walls, stock and one approach is worth more than any journey. A man of seventy with bad hips will not survive a fortnight on the road. The road is not safety. It is a different set of risks that happen to be moving.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Nothing, if you have chosen it. This rule exists to stop the rest of the chapter from becoming a command to run, because running is what people do when frightened and it is not always right. Weigh what you actually have: water, walls, exits, neighbours, and legs. If the answer is that your ground is better than the road, then say so out loud to the people in your house, and stop relitigating it every evening. Deciding to stay and then half staying is the worst of the three.

quote: Assume every sound you make travels twice as far as you think.
what_it_buys_you: A working margin. Sound carries further at night, further in cold air, further along water and much further down a valley than daytime intuition allows for. Every person who has tested this has been shocked by the result. Send somebody half a mile down the lane at ten at night and have them tell you what they can hear of your house. The answer is the rule.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will draw things towards you while believing you are being careful, which is worse than being careless, because careless people stay alert. The families that were overrun in the first winter were not loud households. They were households that had decided they were quiet ones, on no evidence, and had stopped checking. Test it from outside. Everything else in this chapter is guesswork until you have.

quote: Cook before dusk.
what_it_buys_you: The smell and smoke of your kitchen are released into the one part of the day when the air is still moving and light hides nothing that dark would hide anyway. Cooking in daylight, eating at dusk and having a cold, dark, quiet house from nightfall onwards is the single largest change a household can make, and it costs nothing but habit.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Cooking smells at night travel down a valley on the cold air with nothing to compete with them. They can be picked up at a distance that will not seem credible. Stand in a lane and smell somebody else's meal from a quarter of a mile away. Ruth's household ate at four in the afternoon for three years. The people who kept eating at seven kept being visited, and never worked out why.

quote: One lamp, one room, and cover the window before you strike the match.
what_it_buys_you: Light, which people give up too readily and then live worse for. You do not have to sit in the dark. You have to make a single room lightproof, do it properly with battens and blankets rather than a curtain, and check it from the yard once. Then that room can have a lamp in it every night of the winter and the house stays black from the lane.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A candle behind an ordinary curtain is visible for a mile and a half across open country and it is the only light in the landscape. Nothing else advertises occupancy like it, and it advertises to people as much as to anything else. The order of the rule matters and is the part people get wrong: cover first, then light. Doing it the other way round means you have already broadcast for the ninety seconds it takes to hang the blanket.

quote: A dog is a decision, not a companion.
what_it_buys_you: Honesty about a trade that people make without noticing they have made it. A dog is the best early warning system available and is worth more than any watch rota. A dog is also a thing that barks at the wrong moment, needs feeding, and cannot be told to be silent when it matters. Elin's position was that a working dog that has been trained to stop on command is an asset and an untrained one is a liability with a face you love.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Two households I know of were emptied because of a dog, and both of them had been told and had made the reasonable human choice. If you keep the dog, train it in the first month while you still have food to train with, and understand what you are keeping. If you cannot train it, you are choosing company over warning, and that is a real choice that people are allowed to make. Make it with your eyes open.

quote: Never run where you can walk, and never walk where you can wait.
what_it_buys_you: Running is the loudest thing a person does, and it turns one problem into three. A running human is visible at distance and is understood by everything that sees it. Walking is quiet, is thinking speed, and can be stopped. Waiting is free. Deniz reckoned that four out of every five situations he had been in would have resolved on their own if the person had stood still for a hundred seconds.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A hundred yards of panic and you are somewhere you have not chosen, breathing hard, with no idea what is behind you. The rule is not about courage. It is about the fact that the first movement is almost always a reaction, and reactions in this world are expensive. Stop. Count to a hundred. Then move at a walk.

quote: Metal on stone carries further than a voice.
what_it_buys_you: The specific knowledge of which noises are the dangerous ones, which is not intuitive. Human speech at conversational volume is absorbed by hedges and walls and is a poor traveller. A dropped pan, a bolt thrown on a gate, a spade struck on a flag, a car door: these are metallic, sharp, and belong to nothing in a landscape. Wrap what you carry. Tape the buckles. Aiden lined his pack with a jumper for two years.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will be careful about the wrong thing. Households whisper indoors and then hang a metal bucket on a gatepost. Walk your own yard and find every hard surface that can be struck by accident in the dark, and deal with all of them in an afternoon. It is the cheapest hour of work in this book.

quote: Fix the hinge before it needs fixing.
what_it_buys_you: A place that does not announce its own use. Every gate you open twenty times a day, every door, every latch, every board on a stair. Tom greased everything at Hillfoot on a schedule and it sounded like nothing at all, and I did not understand why he bothered until I stayed somewhere that had not.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will start avoiding your own infrastructure. That is the real cost and it takes months to show. People stop using the near gate because it squeals, so they walk the long way round in the open. They stop going to the store after dark because of the door, so they carry a week of food at a time and lose the ability to move at night. A place that is noisy in small ways slowly bends everybody's behaviour into worse shapes, and nobody ever names the hinge.

quote: Smoke is a letter with your address on it.
what_it_buys_you: Warmth, if you are clever about it, and the whole of the second winter for the households that were. Burn dry wood and only dry wood. Burn it hot and fast rather than smouldering it all day. Burn in the middle of the day, when the sky is white and there is weather about. Never on a still, clear, cold morning, when a column will stand up three hundred feet and be visible from the far side of the valley.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The most reliable way to find people in this country is to stand somewhere high at seven in the morning and look. Sam did it for the Bracewell people as a survey and mapped eleven occupied houses in a single hour, none of which knew they were visible. Green wood and a banked fire produce a white smoke that hangs and does not disperse. That is the signature everybody looks for, and it is the one produced by a household trying to make its fuel last.

quote: Keep something loud that you are allowed to do.
what_it_buys_you: A household that can bear its own discipline. Joyce ran a singing hour on Sunday afternoons in a stone cellar with two doors shut. She took a great deal of quiet mockery for it in the first year and none at all in the second. Every rule in this chapter is a small tax on being a person, and a year of paying it without relief produces households that are silent, careful, obedient and coming apart at the seams.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Children who whisper. Adults who flinch at a dropped spoon. Arguments about nothing at ten at night, which is what unspent fear turns into. Two of the households that failed in the second winter did not fail to anything outside their walls. Pick your hour, pick your room, do it properly with the doors shut and somebody on the lane, and then be as loud as you like inside it. The point of surviving is not to become something that cannot sing.

quote: Boil it.
what_it_buys_you: Nearly everything. A rolling boil kills what is in the water in this country. It needs no filter, no chemical, no fuel you do not have, and no judgement you are not qualified to make. It was the first of the seven rules on the parlour door, and it is two words long. The man who wrote it understood that a rule you have to remember correctly under pressure has already failed.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Four days on a floor, and the household around you cutting its own throat trying to nurse you with the same water. The lie the eye tells is the whole problem: it looked clean, it was moving, it came off the fell. All true, and none of it relevant. Boil the water that came off the fell. Boil the water from the tap that still runs. Boil it when you are tired. That is the rule.

quote: Two containers, and they never touch.
what_it_buys_you: A system that cannot be broken by tiredness. One vessel for raw water, one for boiled, marked differently, kept in different places, never swapped and never nested inside each other for storage. Marta painted the raw ones red with fence paint. A household that has done this can be exhausted, ill and working in the dark and still not poison itself, because the correct action is the only available action.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will do everything right for eleven weeks and then pour boiled water into the can that carried the dirty, at night, and undo all of it. This is the most common single failure I know of and it is never committed by careless people. It is committed by tired ones, at the end of a long day, in a kitchen with one clean surface. Design for the tired version of yourself. She is the one who will be doing this.

quote: Site the latrine downhill of the water and twice as far away as feels necessary.
what_it_buys_you: Permanence. Thirty metres from any well, spring, beck or standing water, downhill, downwind, and dug deep with the spoil kept beside it to cover each use. Do it in the first week while it is a matter of choosing, and you have solved it for years. Sam's figure was thirty metres and he was scathing about people who negotiated with him about the last ten of them in the rain.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A hillside is not a diagram. Water moves under it, along the rock, in directions you cannot see from the surface, and it will arrive in your spring six weeks after you made a decision you have since forgotten making. That gap is why nobody ever connects the two. Two households on the Slaidburn road spent a winter ill and blamed the flour. It was not the flour.

quote: Wash your hands before you eat, every time, with no exceptions and no soap.
what_it_buys_you: The largest single reduction in illness available to a household, for the cost of a jug and thirty seconds. Soap helps and its absence is not an excuse: running water over hands with vigorous rubbing removes most of what matters, and the mechanical part is doing most of the work. Ash and water is a serviceable soap and you have ash.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The whole route from latrine to hand to bread to family, which is the route that empties houses. Marta's argument at Whitewell was that no other intervention gives so much for so little. She pushed for a jug at the door of every eating room, not a rule people had to remember. Make it a fixture and not a virtue. Virtue is not there on the bad days.

quote: Rain is the cheapest water you will ever have.
what_it_buys_you: Volume, off any roof, from any weather, without a journey. A shed roof and two butts will keep a household in washing and stock water through most of the year in this country, which means your drinking water and your carrying trips are for drinking alone. Boil what you drink anyway. Birds use the roof too.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Every litre you did not catch is a litre somebody walks for, and walking for water is the most dangerous routine activity in this book. It is predictable. It happens at the same time each day. It goes to a place other people also need, and it is done by somebody carrying weight with both hands full. Cut the number of trips and you cut the exposure, and the roof does it while you sleep.

quote: Never drink from still water, whatever it looks like.
what_it_buys_you: A simple rule for choosing a source when you have no way of testing one. Moving water in the hills, above habitation, above stock, taken from the middle rather than the edge, is the best you will find. Elin's veterinary eye was on the ground above the source: what grazes there, what is dead in it, what drains into it after rain.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Still water concentrates everything that has entered it and adds its own. A tarn, a trough, a flooded ditch, the pool below a ford where cattle stand. All of them look calmer and cleaner than a peaty beck, and the peaty beck is the safer drink by a distance that is not close. Colour is not contamination. Stillness is.

quote: Put the water on a rota and never let one person own it.
what_it_buys_you: A household that keeps working when somebody is ill. That is precisely when the water job matters most, and when the person who has always done it is on the floor. Everybody fetches, everybody boils, everybody knows where the site is and how the containers are marked. Ruth ran hers on a fortnightly rotation with a written list.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Water goes unfetched on the exact day it is most needed, and somebody improvises, and the improvisation is what kills. There is a second cost that is slower and worse. A household where one person carries every load builds a quiet resentment. It comes out in the second winter as something else, and it will look like an argument about cooking.

quote: Filter for grit, boil for life, and do not confuse the two.
what_it_buys_you: Clarity about what your equipment does. Cloth, sand and charcoal take out silt, leaf and much of the taste, and they make water pleasant to drink and easier to boil. They do not make it safe. Sam built beautiful slow sand filters at Bracewell and put a sign on every one of them saying this water is not yet drinkable.
what_ignoring_it_costs: People trust apparatus. Give a household a filter that produces clear water out of brown, and within a month somebody will be drinking straight from the tap on it. It looks like a machine, and machines feel like a warranty. That sign is the whole reason nobody at Bracewell ever did. Filter first if you like. Then boil, every time, without an argument.

quote: A dirty person who is drinking beats a clean one who is not.
what_it_buys_you: Priorities, on the day the whole system fails. If you have one pan of water and a choice between washing and drinking, drink. If you have a source you distrust and no fire, drink it and be ill later. The person who refuses to drink for two days in August will be past making decisions by the evening of the second. Bibi was a pharmacist and she had watched people become fastidious about exactly the wrong thing.
what_ignoring_it_costs: This chapter, taken as scripture, has killed people. There was a man on the Ribble who would not drink from a beck he could not boil. He walked eleven miles in July looking for a better one. He was found four fields from a spring. The rules above are for the ordinary weeks, which is almost all of them. On the day that is not ordinary, drink the water.

quote: Every wound is dirty. Treat it as dirty.
what_it_buys_you: The right starting assumption, which does more than any technique. Clean water, a lot of it, poured with height and force rather than dabbed. Get out the grit, the wool, the thread, the fragment of gate. Marta's line was that irrigation is ninety per cent of wound care and that everybody wants to skip to the interesting part, which is the dressing, because the dressing feels like treatment and washing feels like tidying.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A closed wound with dirt under it, which is a warm dark container for the thing that will kill the person. It will look fine for two days. That is the cruel part and the reason the rule has to be an assumption rather than a judgement, because on the day you decide a wound looks clean enough you will be wrong at a rate of about one in twenty, and one in twenty over three years is everybody you know.

quote: Clean water and pressure beat every ointment in the house.
what_it_buys_you: A correct order of operations when your instinct is reaching for a bottle. Bleeding stops with firm direct pressure held for ten minutes by a clock and not by feel, and almost nobody holds it long enough. After that, water. The tube of antiseptic cream in the drawer is close to irrelevant, and Bibi was blunt about honey, spirits, iodine and every other favourite: they are arguments about the last five per cent.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Time spent on the wrong thing at the only moment when the right thing works. She watched a man lose a hand over a fortnight that started with a farm injury and a cupboard full of remedies applied one after another to a wound nobody had washed. Hold pressure. Then wash it properly, with more water than seems reasonable. Then dress it and leave it alone.

quote: Draw a line round the redness and write the time on the skin.
what_it_buys_you: Evidence instead of impression. A pen line at the edge of the red, with the hour beside it, turns a vague worry into a measurement, and it means the person who looks at four in the afternoon is comparing against a fact rather than against what they remember from breakfast. Spreading beyond the line, red tracking up the limb, heat, swelling, or a fever coming on: those are the signals, and the line is what makes them visible.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Two days. Infection is a race and every treatment available to us works better early, so the entire value of watching is in noticing sooner. Households without the line always report the same thing afterwards, which is that it seemed to happen overnight. It never happens overnight. It happens over four days in front of people who have no way to compare Tuesday with Thursday.

quote: Antibiotics are a course or they are nothing.
what_it_buys_you: A stock that still works in a year. Whatever you have, use it when it is needed and then use all of it, at the intervals, to the end, even after the person feels better on day three. Bibi kept hers behind a locked door and made every request go through a conversation, and she refused far more often than she agreed.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Half a course clears the easy part of an infection and educates the rest, and the person is ill again in a fortnight with something that no longer answers to the only drug in the valley. That is not a private decision. It spends a resource that belongs to everybody, and there is no more of it coming. The other cost is hoarding: tablets kept in a damp drawer for the day they are needed are usually past use by the time somebody is dying in front of you.

quote: Teeth will take more of you than anything with teeth.
what_it_buys_you: Attention to the thing that is coming for everybody and is entirely preventable. Brush with a stick and ash or salt if there is no paste, and keep doing it every day of the winter when nobody can see you and it feels absurd. A tooth abscess is a serious infection nine inches from the brain, in a place where nobody can treat it, and it arrives on a schedule dictated by two years of neglect.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Elin had pulled teeth from cattle and ended up pulling them from people, without anaesthetic, on a kitchen table, four times in the second year. She described it as the worst thing she has done and said that every one of the four was avoidable eighteen months earlier by a person spending ninety seconds a day on something they could not see the point of. Sugar and neglect. That is the whole mechanism.

quote: A bite is not a diagnosis, and it is never yours to pass sentence on.
what_it_buys_you: A household that does not turn on itself in its worst hour. The rule as written has three parts: the bitten person is nursed and not restrained; they are asked what they want while they are still able to say it; and no decision about them is made by one person alone. The Whitewell list is the only document in this book that was written by a committee, and it took them nine hours.
what_ignoring_it_costs: I could fill the chapter. Two brothers on the Bolton road, one of whom was bitten by a dog. A woman locked in an outbuilding for six days over an injury nobody could identify who died of dehydration in there while the household argued about her. Fear does the sentencing, and fear is always in a hurry, and it is always certain. Whatever you believe about what a bite means, the household that decides in an hour, without the person's voice in it, will get it wrong more often than the household that waits and watches. And getting it wrong here is not a mistake you can put down afterwards.

quote: Fever is a clock. Start it at the first shiver.
what_it_buys_you: A record, and a threshold you have agreed on in advance. Write the time of the first rigour, then the state every four hours on paper: hot or cold, drinking or not, talking sense or not, passing water or not. That last one is the most useful sign available without equipment, and it is the one everybody forgets to ask about.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Decisions made from panic at three in the morning about a person who has actually been improving since midnight, or the reverse, which is worse. Bibi would not release anything from the store without the paper, and she was thought hard for it. The paper meant that the household asking her had already looked properly, and it meant she could tell the difference between a fever that was going somewhere and one that was not.

quote: Whoever is nursing eats and sleeps first.
what_it_buys_you: A second week of care. Nursing is a job of days and it is done at night, and the person doing it stops eating without noticing because there is always something else to do. Ruth ran it as a rota with hard reliefs and sent people to bed when their shift ended whether or not they wanted to go. It sounds cold. It is the reason the sick at Bracewell were still being turned at the end of a fortnight.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The nurse goes down, and now you have two patients and nobody who knows the history. The households that lost the most people in the second winter were not the ones with the most illness. They were the ones where one person, almost always the same person, tried to hold all of it alone and was on the floor by the ninth day.

quote: You are allowed to stop treating and start comforting.
what_it_buys_you: A better death, which is a real thing to be able to give somebody and which most of us have forgotten is a choice at all. Warmth, water, clean bedding, light, company, and somebody holding a hand: those are all available to us. Hanna sat with eleven people and said afterwards that she had never once regretted stopping and had regretted continuing three times.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Days of pain spent on interventions that were not going to work, and a family that spends its last hours with somebody arguing about a treatment instead of talking to them. There is a moment when the honest answer is that this person is dying, and everything after it is about how. Recognising the moment is not giving up and it is not something to be ashamed of. This is the exit from this chapter, and it is the one I have needed most.

quote: Eat the perishable first, in order, and write the order on the wall.
what_it_buys_you: Weeks of food that would otherwise rot in front of you. Freezer, then fridge, then fresh, then root and dry store, then tins, in that sequence, with the list written up where everybody can see it so that nobody is deciding at the cupboard door. Ruth's board had three columns and a date beside each item and it fed nine people through a summer.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Households eat what they fancy, which means they eat the tins because tins feel like the emergency ration, and the fresh food spoils while they are protecting the food that would have kept for four years. This is the most common error of the first fortnight and it is committed out of prudence. Eat in the order that things go bad. Save what does not.

quote: Salt is worth more than ammunition.
what_it_buys_you: Preservation, which is the entire difference between a good autumn and a hungry March. Meat, fish, beans, cabbage, hide. Salt is heavy, cheap while there is any, and impossible to make in this country in any quantity, and there is a note in the stock book from the first winter that reads simply: get salt, all of it, now, in a hand that is noticeably less steady than the rest.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A glut you cannot hold. The second autumn was extraordinary. There was more meat in this valley in October than we could eat, and by December there was very little, because it had been eaten fresh or lost, and the households with salt went into the spring with a barrel and the others went into it with nothing. Trade for salt. Take it from every kitchen you pass. It does not spoil and it never gets cheaper.

quote: Never eat the seed.
what_it_buys_you: Next year, and the year after. Seed potatoes, grain, beans held back for sowing, and the two ewes you do not kill. Tom kept his separate, in a locked stone store, labelled, and treated the store as though it were not food at all, which is the only way anybody manages it. It is a small quantity that stands between a household and permanent dependence.
what_ignoring_it_costs: In February the seed store is the best food in the house and there is a hungry child in it, and I am not going to pretend that this is a straightforward rule to keep. But a household that eats its seed has converted a farm into three good meals, and there is nothing after that except asking somebody else for seed on their terms, and their terms in March are not the terms they would have offered in October. Tom's answer was to make the decision structural. Lock it. Give the key to somebody who will not be in the kitchen at midnight.

quote: Hunger makes bad plans look reasonable. Eat before you decide.
what_it_buys_you: Judgement at the moment it is worth most. A hungry group will talk itself into a raid, a river crossing, a trade with people it does not trust, or a walk to a rumour, and will experience all of that as clear thinking. Deniz would not hold a planning conversation before a meal, and the rule at his table was that anybody who suggested something ambitious got a bowl before an answer.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The worst decisions of the second winter were all made at the end of the day, by people who had eaten once, about food. Three of them killed somebody. Hunger does not feel like impairment from inside; it feels like urgency and clarity. That is what makes it more dangerous than tiredness, which at least announces itself.

quote: Learn three wild foods properly instead of thirty badly.
what_it_buys_you: Real calories from things you cannot misidentify. Nettle, which is everywhere and is unmistakable and holds up boiled. Hawthorn leaf in spring. Fish, if you have water. Elin's whole argument was about confidence under pressure: three plants you know absolutely, in quantity, in all their stages, are worth more than a book of thirty you half know, because you will be foraging tired and in poor light.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The foraging books make it look like a larder and it is not. Wild food in this country is a supplement, not a diet, and the calories per hour of searching are terrible compared with a garden or a snare. The households that leaned on it went into the winter light. And there is the other cost, which is rarer and absolute: two deaths in the valley from something eaten by somebody who was fairly sure.

quote: Cache in three places and never all of it anywhere.
what_it_buys_you: Survival of a disaster rather than an inconvenience. Split the store: some in the house, some buried or walled up at a distance, some at a third site nobody discusses. Fire, theft, rot and flood are all single-location events, and a household that loses one third of its food in November is having a bad month, while a household that loses all of it is finished.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Everything, at once, on somebody else's schedule. Aiden had watched three households cleared out in an afternoon in the second summer and every one of them had kept a good store in one dry room, which is exactly what a careful person would do. Keep the third cache genuinely secret and check it twice a year, because the failure mode of a buried cache is that it is wet and nobody looked.

quote: Fat is the thing you run out of.
what_it_buys_you: The winter. A diet of potatoes, roots and greens looks adequate on the plate and leaves people cold, slow and always hungry, and the thing missing is fat. Render everything. Keep the drippings, the marrow, the skin, the tallow. Butter, lard, oil and suet are the highest-value foods you will handle and they are the first things people stop noticing when they disappear.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A household that is eating what looks like enough and is thin by March. Bibi identified it before anybody else because she was watching people rather than stores, and the pattern was always the same: plenty of bulk, no fat, and a slow decline that everybody blamed on the cold. Cold is worse when you have not eaten fat. So is thinking.

quote: A garden sown in March feeds you in August, and not one day sooner.
what_it_buys_you: An accurate calendar, which is the only thing that lets you plan a hungry period rather than discover one. Potatoes go in when the soil warms and come out in late summer. Brassicas sown in June carry you through the winter and have to be started while you are still busy with everything else. The stock book has it all laid out by week, in somebody's handwriting, with what went wrong each year in the margin.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The gap. Between the end of the stored food and the first harvest there is a period of about eight weeks that nobody plans for because it happens in early summer when the countryside looks generous, and it is the hungriest part of the year in every account I have. Count backwards from your harvest. Then look at what you have and decide now, in comfort, how thin June is going to be.

quote: Keep one thing back that is only for pleasure.
what_it_buys_you: People who are still willing to do the work. A jar of something sweet, a bottle, a tin of peaches, tea. Nell kept a box under her bed and produced it four times a year without warning, on bad days, and the effect on a farmhouse in February is out of all proportion to the calories. Nobody has ever worked hard for a life of pure sufficiency.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A household that is provisioned correctly, following every rule in this chapter, and slowly stops caring. That sounds soft next to the rest of the chapter and it is not. The failures I have seen in the third winter were not failures of supply. They were people who could not find a reason to go out in the rain and check the snares, and there is no store in the world that survives a household in that state.

quote: Two doors, always.
what_it_buys_you: The difference between a problem and an ending. Two ways out of every building you sleep in, two ways off every piece of ground, and both of them checked, in the dark, by everybody who lives there. Not a window you could theoretically get through. A route you have walked at night, in boots, carrying something.
what_ignoring_it_costs: One door means one bad afternoon finishes you. This is the rule that appears in every survivor's account I have ever collected, and the one that costs least to keep. A back door unbolted. A ladder left up. A gap in a wall kept clear. Whatever else you do to a building, do not reduce it to a single exit in the name of making it safe. Every improvement that seals a place is also sealing you inside it.

quote: Choose ground for its water first and its walls second.
what_it_buys_you: A place that works for years rather than a place that survives a night. A spring or a beck above the buildings, so it comes to you and does not have to be carried up. Sam's ranking was water, then approach, then exits, then shelter, then walls, and he would not move on the first one. A perfect house that is four hundred yards from water is a house where somebody makes eight hundred trips a year in the open with both hands full.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The slow bleed. Every trip is exposure, every trip is time, and the household adapts by fetching less, which means washing less and drinking less, and you are back in chapter four. Two families in the second year abandoned good stone buildings for worse ones with better water. Both said the same thing afterwards: they should have done it in the first month instead of the fourteenth.

quote: A wall you cannot watch is a wall you do not have.
what_it_buys_you: An honest picture of your own perimeter. Walk it at three in the morning and ask, from the kitchen window, what you can see and what you would hear. A hundred yards of good stone wall behind a barn where nobody ever looks is not protecting you; it is telling you a story about being protected while somebody stands behind it.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Effort spent in the wrong place. People build. It is satisfying, visible work that feels like progress, and households will spend a fortnight raising a barrier they cannot observe rather than an afternoon cutting the hedge that blinds them. Deniz's version was blunter than mine: you do not need a wall, you need to know. Watch first. Build only where watching has told you to.

quote: Cut the sightlines before you build anything.
what_it_buys_you: Distance, which is the only resource that matters when somebody arrives. Take out the hedge that hides the bend, the shed that blocks the view of the lane, the elder in the corner of the yard. Four hundred yards of warning is enough for a household to be inside, quiet and counting. Forty yards is enough to be surprised at.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Every problem arrives at arm's length. There is a caution attached, and Bracewell learned it the hard way. Land you have cleared is also land you are visible on, and a farm stripped of every hedge announces itself as a farm somebody is holding. Cut what blinds you on your own approaches. Leave the screen that hides your roof from the ridge. It is a trade, not a principle, and the orders are wrong to state it as flatly as they do.

quote: Upstairs is a trap with a view.
what_it_buys_you: A correct use for the first floor, which is watching, and a correct place to sleep, which is not up there. Height is the best observation you have and the worst position you can be caught in. Aiden scavenged houses for two years and had a rule about never going above ground level in a building he had not first walked the outside of.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A staircase is a corridor with one end. Everybody who has been trapped in a building in this valley was trapped upstairs, and in three of those cases the ground floor was clear and stayed clear the whole time. Use the height in the day. Sleep near a door. If you must sleep upstairs, put a rope on the window sill and leave it there, and check the knot in daylight now and again.

quote: Make every route in noisy on purpose.
what_it_buys_you: Warning that works while you are asleep, for the price of an afternoon. Gravel on the two paths people would actually use. A gate that is wired so it rattles. Tins on a line across the gap in the wall. Tom did it in the second month, and he did the thing most people miss. He left one silent route for his own household, so they were not setting off their own alarms four times a night.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A watch rota that has to be kept by human beings, all night, in winter, for years. That is the alternative and it is not sustainable; watches degrade, people doze, and the third winter is when it happens. Passive warning does not get tired. It is also the only thing that protects you on the night everybody is ill.

quote: Fire ends places. Plan for it before it is on you.
what_it_buys_you: The one disaster that can finish a well-run household in twenty minutes. Water in the yard where it can be reached without going through the building. A break between the store and the house. Nothing burning left unattended, ever, and the stove out at night. The school log has eleven pages about a chimney and then stops.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Everything you have built and everybody asleep in it. We are all burning wood indoors in buildings wired for a different century, with candles and lamps and no water above the ground floor, and we are doing it while exhausted. Fire is more likely to kill you now than it was before, by a long way. It receives the least attention in every household I have visited, including my own until the school burned.

quote: Do not fortify what you cannot leave.
what_it_buys_you: A clear head about a thing people become sentimental about. Three years of work makes a place into an argument you cannot lose. Deniz tested every improvement against one question. Does this make it harder for us to walk out of here in ten minutes. Barred windows fail that test. A dug well passes it. Stored food in one cellar fails it, which is chapter six's third cache.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will stay when you should go, and you will not experience it as a mistake. You will experience it as loyalty to the place. Everybody who died at the mill died because the mill was worth defending, and it was, and they were right about that, and it did not matter.

quote: The place is worth less than the people in it, and you will not believe that when it matters.
what_it_buys_you: Permission, decided in advance, on a calm day, in front of witnesses. Ruth made her household say it out loud once a year: this is a building, we are not going to die in it, and if we go the seed and the medicine and the children go first and the rest stays. Say it while nothing is happening. It will not be sayable later.
what_ignoring_it_costs: This rule contradicts the one before it and the whole of chapter two, and I have left all three of them standing. Some ground is worth holding and Tom was right to hold it. But every household that lost people to a place lost them the same way, which is by making a decision to leave four hours after the decision was available. The building will still be there in a month. You can come back. Nobody has ever come back to a person.

quote: Talk first, from a distance, with something solid between you.
what_it_buys_you: Time, and the ability to change your mind. Sixty yards, a wall, a raised voice, and a conversation that begins before anybody is committed. Almost every situation that goes wrong between two groups goes wrong inside fifteen feet, in the first ninety seconds, because both sides were surprised and both were frightened and somebody moved a hand.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will make a decision about eight people in the time it takes them to cross a yard. Deniz's whole method was to slow the encounter down: talk across a distance for five minutes about nothing, the weather, the road, where they have come from, and let both sides get bored. Boredom is the thing you are trying to manufacture. Nobody has ever been killed by a group they had already been bored with.

quote: Never meet anybody at your own gate.
what_it_buys_you: A meeting place of your choosing, which is worth more than any weapon. Bracewell used a bend in the lane three hundred yards out with a wall on one side, and every conversation with an outsider happened there. It shows nothing, commits nothing, and gives you a walk home during which you can talk it over.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Everything you own becomes part of the negotiation. At your own gate they can see the roof, the stock, the store, the children, the number of you, and whether the men are older than they look, and all of that is now in the head of somebody you may never see again, or may see in four months with company. Meet away from the place. Always. Even for people you like.

quote: Feed them outside the wall.
what_it_buys_you: The ability to be decent without being opened. Bread, hot water, a bag of potatoes, and directions, handed over at the meeting place, is a real kindness and costs you almost nothing, and it is what the great majority of people at your gate actually need. Ruth did it more than a hundred times and never once regretted it.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The two failure modes are opposite and both are expensive. A household that gives nothing accumulates people who have nothing and know where you are, which is exactly how the group at the mill formed. A household that brings everybody in has lost the only thing that lets it keep giving. Between them there is a wide, workable middle, and Ruth lived in it for three years.

quote: Believe the children.
what_it_buys_you: The most reliable information available at a meeting. Adults arrive with a prepared account because they have learned they must. Children answer what you ask. How many nights have you been walking. Was there a house. Did the men come with you from there. Joyce would talk to the children while somebody else talked to the parents, and she said she had never had a false picture from doing it.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will take an adult's story at face value and it will be a story built to get them in, which is what a frightened parent should be doing and not a sign of bad faith. The rule has a limit that Joyce insisted on: this is for building a picture, not for cross-examining a nine year old about their family in front of them. Ask two gentle questions. That is usually the whole of it.

quote: A group that will not give you a name will not give you anything else.
what_it_buys_you: The single most useful signal at a distance. Names, where you have come from, where you are going, who is hurt. The great majority of people answer these, and answer them at once, because they have nothing to hide and a great deal to gain from being known. Aiden's line was that honest people over-explain and frightened people over-explain more.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You will miss the small number of encounters that are actually dangerous, and they announce themselves early if you are listening for it: no names, questions in both directions but no answers, a count of you being taken, a story that adjusts to what you seem to want. That is a different thing from what a nervous family does, and once you have met it you will not confuse the two.

quote: Trade at distance, in the open, in daylight, or not at all.
what_it_buys_you: Trade, which is worth having, and which almost stopped in the second winter because nobody had a safe shape for it. Neutral ground both parties can see across. Goods set down and stepped back from. Two people, not eight. And an agreement made the meeting before about what is coming, so that nobody is improvising.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The trade that goes wrong is almost always the one arranged quickly, at dusk, at somebody's buildings, with more people present than were expected. Whitewell lost salt and a man in one afternoon by breaking three of the four conditions at once, and the list was written the following week by people who were arguing about whose fault it had been.

quote: Nobody tells the same story twice unless they have rehearsed it.
what_it_buys_you: A quiet check that costs nothing. Ask about the route again an hour later, in a different order, and a true account will come back with different details and the same shape, because that is how memory works. A prepared one comes back word for word, or comes back different in the shape and the same in the words.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Hanna was careful about this and I want to repeat her warning rather than her method. People lie for good reasons. A family that has been turned away from four places will have learned a story that works, and the fact that it is polished does not make them dangerous, it makes them experienced. The signal is worth having and it is not a verdict. Use it to ask a better question, not to close the gate.

quote: Never let anybody see the whole of what you have.
what_it_buys_you: A margin that survives your own generosity. Whatever is visible from the meeting place is what you are known to have, so the store is out of sight, the stock is in the back field on the days you are expecting anybody, and the third cache is a thing nobody outside the household has ever heard mentioned. Tom went further and kept a small obvious store that could be given away.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You become a number in other people's plans. This is the rule that sounds least generous and is actually what makes generosity survivable, because a household that is known to be thin can afford to give a stranger bread, while a household that has been seen to be rich will be visited by the fifth group in a way the first four did not consider.

quote: Take somebody in, or admit what you are becoming.
what_it_buys_you: A household you would want to survive into. Everyone in this valley who is still here is here because at some point somebody who owed them nothing opened a gate. Marta's position, and she argued it hard at Whitewell against people with better reasons than hers, was that a household which has decided in principle never to take anybody in has already made its decision about the rest of it too, and will keep making that decision until there is nothing left inside the wall worth the walls.
what_ignoring_it_costs: She was not naive and she was not talking about taking in everybody, which is not possible and gets people killed. She was talking about the third winter, and about what a household becomes after a hundred consecutive refusals: quiet, efficient, sealed, and unable to remember why it is doing any of this. We took in four people that Marta argued for. Two of them are the reason Hillfoot came through the second winter. One of them wrote a third of the chapter you have just read.

quote: Write the rules down before you need them, and put them where they can be read.
what_it_buys_you: Arguments about a document instead of arguments about a person. Once it is on a wall, disagreement is directed at nine lines of paint rather than at whoever is standing in the kitchen, and the thing can be amended in daylight by people who have eaten. It also means that everybody who joins the group learns the rules in the first hour rather than in their first row.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Every dispute becomes personal and every precedent has to be argued from scratch. Unwritten rules always exist, they are just held differently by each person, and the discovery that they differ happens in the middle of a crisis. The nine lines took Bracewell an evening. Nothing else they did bought so much for so little.

quote: Somebody has the final word in an emergency, and everybody agrees who before there is one.
what_it_buys_you: Ninety seconds, which is the whole of an emergency. It does not need to be the same person for everything, and Bracewell had three: one for anything outside the wall, one for anything medical, one for fire. Named, agreed, written up, and holding only until the thing is over.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A committee in a yard at night with something coming up the lane. Deniz had seen it and described it as the worst thing he had ever watched: eleven capable adults, all of them right, none of them able to move, losing four minutes. The rule is not about hierarchy and it collapses if it becomes hierarchy. It is about a temporary, bounded authority that ends when the noise stops, and about everyone knowing which voice to obey without checking whose it is.

quote: The person who holds the food does not also hold the rota.
what_it_buys_you: Trust that does not depend on anybody's character. Split the jobs that carry power: stores, work allocation, the medicine, the decision to trade. Different people, rotated on a known cycle, each of them counted in front of somebody else. Ruth's design assumed that everybody was decent and that being decent would not be enough.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Suspicion, which is slower and more destructive than theft and does not need any theft to happen. A single person who decides who works and who eats will be believed to be favouring somebody within about two months, and they may well be, because they are a human being deciding those things about people they like unevenly. Do not ask anybody to be that good. Split it.

quote: Everybody works, including the ones who cannot.
what_it_buys_you: People who are still part of the group. The old, the injured, the ill and the very young all have work available to them: watching, sorting, mending, teaching, minding, peeling, keeping the log. Joyce had a woman of eighty-one who could not walk to the gate and who ran the entire seed inventory and taught four children to read.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Two things at once. The group loses hours it needs. And the person loses their place in it, which happens fast, and after a fortnight of being carried they will start apologising for eating, and then they will start refusing food, and I have seen where that goes twice. Give everybody a job that genuinely matters and let them do it badly if that is how it gets done.

quote: Say the bad news at breakfast.
what_it_buys_you: A group that can absorb it. Bad news delivered in the morning, to everybody at once, in plain words, gets a day of daylight and work to be metabolised in. The same news at nine at night sits in the dark with people and comes out as something else entirely by morning.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Rumour, which is always worse than the fact and always arrives anyway. Hanna's rule came out of the second winter when a decision about the stores was taken quietly by three people who were trying to avoid frightening anybody, and it was known in an inaccurate form within a day and a half, and the version that circulated was so much worse than the truth that two families left. Tell them at breakfast. Tell them the actual number.

quote: A grievance kept for a fortnight is no longer about the thing.
what_it_buys_you: Small problems that stay small. There is an entry in the log, in a teacher's handwriting, listing three arguments and the number of days each had been running before it was raised, and the conclusion at the bottom is that nothing raised in the first two days had ever needed more than a conversation. Have a way of raising things that does not require courage: a weekly hour, a person whose job it is, anything.
what_ignoring_it_costs: In a group of nine people who cannot leave, a fortnight is long enough for an irritation about washing up to become a settled belief about somebody's character, and once it is about character it cannot be resolved by fixing the washing up. Everything I have watched come apart came apart at that stage and not before.

quote: Count the stores in front of two people, on a fixed day.
what_it_buys_you: A number everybody believes, which is the foundation of every hard decision you are going to have to make together. First Sunday of the month, two people, written in the book, read out at breakfast. Sam argued for it not because he expected theft but because he expected disbelief, and disbelief is the thing that actually breaks a group.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A household where everybody is privately estimating, and where the estimates diverge, and where the people who think there is less are hoarding and the people who think there is more are resentful of the rationing. Bracewell's count took twenty minutes a month. Sam's phrase for it was that the count is not an audit, it is a conversation everybody is allowed to be in.

quote: Nobody watches alone for more than two hours.
what_it_buys_you: A watch that is actually being kept. Attention collapses after about two hours in the cold and dark, and the person on watch does not notice it collapsing, which is the whole difficulty. Short shifts, a proper handover with something said out loud, and a warm place to go afterwards.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Four hours of theatre. A household that runs long watches has people sitting in the dark achieving nothing, sleeping worse, working worse the next day, and providing a sense of security that is not connected to anything. Tom would rather have had passive warning on the approaches and everybody asleep than a man out for six hours, and after the second winter that is what he did.

quote: You are allowed to leave.
what_it_buys_you: The thing that makes all of the above voluntary. A group people cannot leave is a different kind of place, and it becomes that kind of place by degrees without anybody choosing it. Bracewell wrote down what a person takes with them when they go, which was their own gear, a fortnight of food and a share of the seed, and agreed it in a good month so that nobody had to negotiate it in a bad one.
what_ignoring_it_costs: People stay in groups that are going wrong, and they stay for the reason that leaving means starving, and a group that knows its members cannot leave stops having to be worth staying in. Aiden left two places in his first year and both of them tried to keep him and one of them took his boots. Write down the terms of leaving. Then hope nobody uses them.

quote: Wet kills. Cold only helps it.
what_it_buys_you: The correct enemy. A dry person in bad clothes at freezing will be uncomfortable for a long time and will live. A wet person in good clothes at eight degrees is on a clock, and eight degrees and raining is the ordinary weather here for five months. Everything about a winter routine should be built around getting dry and staying dry: a drying place, a spare set, and a hard rule about changing.
what_ignoring_it_costs: People will work all day in the wet because they are not cold while they are working, and the bill arrives when they stop. Deniz put the drying rack in the kitchen at Bracewell and made it the most valuable square yard in the building. He made changing out of wet clothes a rule and not a choice. The person who most needs to change is always the one who says they are fine.

quote: Heat the person, then the bed, then the room. Never the house.
what_it_buys_you: A winter's fuel that lasts a winter. Warm clothes and a hat indoors, a hot stone or a bottle in the bed an hour before it is used, one room with the door shut, and everything else left to the weather. Sam reckoned the difference between heating a room and heating a farmhouse was a factor of six in wood, which is the difference between cutting in October and cutting in January.
what_ignoring_it_costs: You burn the whole store by the middle of February trying to make a stone building comfortable, which it will not become. Then you are cold in the worst month with nothing left and a green woodpile. The households that were warm in the second winter were not the ones with the most wood. They were the ones living in one room and wearing coats in it.

quote: Cut your wood a year before you burn it.
what_it_buys_you: Twice the heat and a quarter of the smoke, which is chapter three's problem solved as a side effect. Green wood has half its weight in water and burns cold, dirty and slow, and it lines a chimney with the thing that later burns the house down. A year under cover, split, off the ground. Tom worked two winters ahead and always had.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A cold February with a full woodpile, which is the most demoralising thing I have watched a household go through. They did the work. They cut, hauled, split and stacked four tons, and it will not burn properly, and there is no fixing it now. This is the purest example in the book of a rule about time rather than effort. You cannot work harder in January to undo not having cut in the previous January.

quote: Two pairs of dry socks are a survival stock.
what_it_buys_you: Feet you can still walk on in March. Wool, changed daily, dried by the fire overnight, with the wet pair going inside your coat during the day if there is no fire. Aiden had four pairs and treated them the way other people treated the medicine box, and he walked more miles than anybody in this valley and never had a foot problem.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Trench foot, which nobody expects and which took three people out of action for weeks in the second winter, and one of them permanently. It comes from days of damp rather than from cold, and it arrives without pain until it is well established. Feet, hands and head. Everything else about winter clothing is negotiable and those three are not.

quote: Sleep small and sleep together.
what_it_buys_you: The eight hours a day when you are producing no heat and losing it fastest. A small room, a low ceiling or a canopy over the bed, bodies together, straw or bracken under the mattress rather than a cold floor beneath it. Ruth put nine people in two rooms at Bracewell and there was some grumbling about it in the first November and none at all by January.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A household that is cold all night for five months does not recover during the day. It shows up as illness, accidents, short tempers and a general slowness that everybody blames on the diet. This is also the cheapest of all the winter rules. It costs nothing at all except the idea that adults are entitled to their own rooms, which is a thing worth having and not worth a winter.

quote: Do the outside jobs in November.
what_it_buys_you: A January you can survive on the inside. Roof, gutters, drains, gate, wall gaps, the path to the store, the woodshed door, and the state of the boots, all done while there is still light and the ground is workable. The stock book has a November list four pages long and a January list with six items on it, and the discipline is in the difference.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Every one of those jobs done in the wet, in the dark, badly, by somebody who is already cold, at the exact moment when the failure of any of them is most expensive. A blocked drain in November is a morning's work. In February it is a flooded store, a fortnight of damp and a household eating wet flour.

quote: Nobody travels alone between December and March.
what_it_buys_you: Somebody to fetch help. Winter travel here is not dangerous because of what is on the road. It is dangerous because a turned ankle four miles out at three in the afternoon is a night outside. A night outside in January is not survivable in the clothes people actually wear. Elin lost a colleague that way in the first year on a journey of five miles that she had made forty times.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The whole margin. A pair can carry an injured person, keep them warm, or leave one and go, and any of the three is a survivable afternoon. Alone, all of it is the same afternoon. The rule has one exception and it is not the one people reach for: a short familiar journey in daylight with somebody at both ends who knows your timing and will come looking. Being expected is the actual protection.

quote: Watch for whoever has gone quiet.
what_it_buys_you: The person you are about to lose to something that is not cold. February in a dark house with the same eleven people is when the grief that everybody has parked since the first spring comes back for its answer. Hanna's method was simple and I have never seen it fail: notice who has stopped talking, and go and sit next to them and do a job together without asking them anything.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Two of the nineteen we lost in the second winter were not lost to the winter. Both had been quiet for a fortnight in a full house. Everyone said afterwards that they had noticed and had not wanted to intrude, which is the most understandable sentence in this book and the most expensive.

quote: You are allowed to spend the winter doing nothing.
what_it_buys_you: Spring, with people left in it. There is no useful outside work for a great deal of January and February in this country. A household that treats the whole winter as a productivity problem will grind through it and arrive at March exhausted, in the month when the year's actual work begins. Joyce's winter timetable had three hours of jobs in it and the rest was reading, teaching, sleeping, cards and talking.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Everything that matters and nothing you can point at. Rest is not idleness and it is not a reward for having earned it. It is the thing that puts a household on its feet in the spring. The seasons in this country have been arranged so that there is a stretch in the middle where the only sensible thing to do is very little. Take it. The list will still be there.

quote: Know which rule you are breaking, and say it out loud first.
what_it_buys_you: The difference between a decision and a drift. Naming it, aloud, to another person, in the moment, takes four seconds and converts an impulse into a choice somebody else has heard. We are lighting a fire in the open. We are going out after dark. Ruth's household did it dozens of times and the saying of it was the whole discipline.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Rules do not get broken. They get eroded, one reasonable exception at a time, until the household is doing something it would never have agreed to do and cannot remember deciding. Nobody at the mill ever voted to stop keeping watch.

quote: Break a rule for a person. Never for a thing.
what_it_buys_you: A test you can apply in twenty seconds under pressure, and the only one in this chapter that has never let me down. Going out at night for somebody who is hurt is a rule worth breaking. Going out at night for a store of flour is not, and it will feel identical while you are pulling your boots on.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Almost everybody who has died breaking a rule in this valley died going back for an object. Fuel, tools, a generator, a box of tins. Every one of those journeys was justified at the time by arithmetic that was correct. The flour is still there. So is the man who went for it.

quote: A rule you learned in the first winter is about the first winter.
what_it_buys_you: Rules that keep up with the world. The valley of the first year had cars in it, open shops, a functioning road east and eleven times as many people. Half the instructions that were correct then are now costing somebody a morning's work for nothing. The stock book has whole pages crossed out with a date and a note beside them.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Effort spent defending against a year that has finished. Review the list once a year, in the quiet part of the winter. Ask of each rule what it is protecting you from, and whether that thing is still out there.

quote: Two of you have to agree. One of you can always keep it.
what_it_buys_you: A brake that does not depend on being the calmest person in the room. Any rule in this book can be broken by a household that agrees to break it, and any single member can refuse and the thing does not happen. It sounds slow. It takes about a minute and it has stopped more bad journeys here than any other arrangement.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The person who is most frightened, most tired or most certain makes the decision, and those three are usually the same person, and they are always the one moving first. Deniz's addition was that the one who refuses does not have to explain, because the requirement to give reasons is how a refusal gets talked out of.

quote: Distrust anybody who has never been wrong.
what_it_buys_you: Protection from the most dangerous person in a group, who is not the reckless one. It is the competent one with a good record, whose judgement everybody has learned to defer to, and who has therefore stopped receiving any correction at all. Colm was that man. He earned it honestly.
what_ignoring_it_costs: A group with one voice in it, which is a group with one point of failure. It is also unkind to the person, who ends up unable to be uncertain in front of anybody and then unable to arrive at a door at night asking for help. If you are the one being deferred to, be wrong out loud about something small, on purpose, in front of everybody, twice a year.

quote: When the rule and the room disagree, believe the room.
what_it_buys_you: Your own eyes back. The rules in this book are averages taken across three years and a whole district. You are standing in one place, looking at one particular thing that none of us has seen. Where the ground in front of you plainly contradicts the page, the ground is the better evidence. It knows about today.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Aiden broke chapter eight's rules to bring two children in through the back field at dusk without meeting anybody at the meeting place first, and by every line of that chapter he was wrong. They are both still here. He also, in the same month, trusted a room over a rule and lost a coat, a bag and a fortnight of food. The room is better evidence. It is not good evidence.

quote: Write down what you broke and what happened.
what_it_buys_you: A book that improves. Every rule in here came from somebody keeping a record, and the exceptions are more informative than the rules. A rule that gets broken four times a year with no consequence is not a rule. It is a habit with a uniform on. Joyce kept the log at Whitewell in a school exercise book.
what_ignoring_it_costs: The same argument every year and nothing learned from any of it. Half the entries in this book are in the shape they are because somebody broke them and wrote down why. Three were removed when the log made it clear they had never once been right.

quote: Four of these are not for breaking.
what_it_buys_you: A floor. Everything in this book is negotiable except four things, and I have chosen them by looking at the ground behind the chapel and not by reasoning about it. Boil the water. Keep the second door. Talk from a distance before anybody moves. And no decision about a human being gets made by one person in a hurry.
what_ignoring_it_costs: These are the four where the cost of being wrong lands on somebody who did not make the decision, and that is the whole basis for the list. Break any of the other ninety-five when the room tells you to. Break these when you have run out of ways of being a person, and not before.

quote: Put this down and go and live.
what_it_buys_you: The point of the exercise. Nell is nineteen now. She has read this list more carefully than anybody and she is scathing about it, and her objection is the correct one. It is a book about not dying, and there is nothing in it about anything else. She has a garden that is not a food garden. She is teaching two children to swim in a river that four of these rules would keep them out of.
what_ignoring_it_costs: Ninety-eight rules will get a household through a winter. They will not give anybody a reason to want the spring. I have watched people learn all of this and keep every line of it, and become careful, and quiet, and unbeatable. By the third year there was nothing left inside the wall except the arrangements for staying alive. That is not survival. It is a slower version of the other thing. Learn the ninety-eight. Then close the book, because it is a list of ways not to die and you were not put here to spend your life reading one.
